text:
FPMC combines user–item preference factors with factorized item–item transitions, providing generalization beyond observed transition counts; FOSSIL combines history-based item similarity with personalized higher-order Markov effects and reports advantages on sparse datasets. These are established comparators for a sparse transition graph. SASRec already learns dependencies on recent actions, so an additive graph’s benefit remains an empirical question. Sources: [FPMC](https://www.ismll.uni-hildesheim.de/pub/pdfs/RendleFreudenthaler2010-FPMC.pdf), [FOSSIL](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.09152), [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781).

A reproducible proposed estimator: count directed adjacent training transitions c(i,j), define destination marginal q(j), and smooth P(j|i)=[c(i,j)+αq(j)]/[Σk c(i,k)+α]. Compare conditional probability against log-lift log[P(j|i)/q(j)]; the latter discounts destination popularity but can amplify weakly supported rare pairs. Use a minimum raw-count threshold, optionally shrink lift by c/(c+τ), and retain top-k outgoing edges. Specify whether pruning changes normalization; retaining original probabilities avoids silently redistributing discarded mass. Aggregate recent-history edges with normalized exponential position weights. These formulas are suggested experimental choices, not a published SASRec hybrid recipe or evidence of improvement.

Establish added value through matched ablations: SASRec alone; popularity and transition-only baselines; SASRec plus conditional probability versus log-lift; adjacent transitions versus unordered co-occurrence; last-item versus recency-weighted history; and FPMC/FOSSIL. Tune smoothing, support, pruning and blend weight using only the pinned four-category macro validation HR@10. Report category scores and graph coverage alongside the macro score; published results under other protocols cannot establish gains on this benchmark.
